          <h1>Welcome to AffineDrift</h1>
          <p class="subtitle">Technical Notes on Golf Mechanics and Control</p>
        </div>

        <div class="welcome-intro">
          <p>
            AffineDrift collects technical articles, textbook chapters, and reference material on multibody dynamics, control, biomechanics, and the golf swing. The site distinguishes established mathematical structure from AffineDrift's own model-dependent interpretations and working hypotheses.
          </p>
          <p>
            The material is organized into two main textbooks, exploratory article series, critique pages, and a reference library of external resources.
          </p>
        </div>
      </section>

            <p>Coaches and analysts will find explicitly defined mechanical thresholds, simulation-backed insights on swing path optimization, and concrete parameter ranges for golf biomechanics.</p>
          </div>
          <div class="audience-card" style="padding: 1.5rem; background: var(--bg-secondary, #f8f9fa); border-radius: 8px; border-top: 4px solid #10b981;">

            <p><strong>Focus:</strong> Intuitive explanations, motivated examples, plain English.</p>
            <p>Look for the "Layman's Terms" boxes throughout our articles, which translate abstract control theory concepts into relatable analogies and real-world golf scenarios without the math.</p>
          </div>

            <p><strong>Focus:</strong> Precise definitions, complete derivations, consistent notation.</p>
            <p>Explore the textbooks and theory articles for rigorous formulations of the golf swing as an affine controllable system, complete with differential dynamic programming (DDP) solutions.</p>
          </div>
        </div>

      <!-- Math Showcase -->
      <section id="framework" class="math-section" style="margin-top: 3rem;">
        <h2>The Core Framework</h2>
        <p>The golf swing can be modeled as a control-affine system:</p>
        <div class="math-showcase">
          $$\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u$$
        </div>
        <p>
          Where <em>f(x)</em> represents the drift dynamics (passive forces including gravity and velocity-dependent inertial coupling terms) and <em>g(x)u</em> represents the controlled torque inputs from the golfer.
        </p>
        <div style="margin-top: 1rem; padding: 0.75rem 1rem; background: var(--bg-secondary, #f8f9fa); border-left: 3px solid var(--primary-color, #2563eb); border-radius: 4px; font-size: 0.9rem; color: var(--text-light, #6b7280);">
          <strong>Provenance:</strong> The control-affine form ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u is standard in nonlinear control theory (Isidori, 1995; Nijmeijer &amp; van der Schaft, 1990). Its application to golf biomechanics — the drift/input decomposition, ZTCF, and DCR — is AffineDrift synthesis. See the <a href="articles/theory-part1.html">Theory Part 1</a> derivation and the <a href="critiques/index.html">Critiques &amp; Responses</a> for scope limitations.
        </div>
      </section>

      <!-- About the Approach Section -->
      <section id="approach" class="approach-section" style="margin-top: 3rem;">
        <h2>AI Methodology and Review Process</h2>
        <div class="approach-content">
          <p>
            AffineDrift represents a novel approach to scientific synthesis: <strong>AI-Assisted Research</strong>. The site is assembled through a highly structured, mixed drafting and review workflow utilizing advanced AI agents to accelerate literature synthesis, code generation, and mathematical derivations.
          </p>
          <p>
            However, all AI outputs are subjected to rigorous constraints: assumptions must be made explicit, and claims must be tied to stated mathematical models or cited sources. Priority is given to material that can be checked directly: equations that can be inspected, code that can be reviewed, and references that can be traced independently.
          </p>
          <p>
            Not every page is at the same editorial stage. Some pages are polished expositions, while others remain exploratory notes or literature-review scaffolds and should be read with the status notes on each page in mind.
          </p>
          <p>
            Critical review is part of the publication model. Limitations, objections, and unresolved evidence gaps are surfaced alongside the main articles in dedicated "Critics' Comments" sections, rather than hidden behind them.
          </p>
        </div>
      </section>
